name: Lake Tesse Trout Translocation (Scandinavian Mesolithic)
summary: Brown trout carried by hand above waterfalls and rapids the fish could not pass, into high-altitude lakes that held none, and harvested with wooden traps. The earliest documented case of humans deliberately moving a species into a new water body — a stocking programme run seven thousand years before anyone farmed in Scandinavia.
longevity_basis: Persistence of the outcome, not continuous operation of the equipment. The wooden traps are radiocarbon-dated from c. 5000 BCE and their use across the whole span is not attested. What has persisted is the introduced ecosystem: self-sustaining brown trout in lakes that had none, still fished today. This entry measures how long the modification lasted, which for an ecological intervention is the property that matters.

claims.statement: Brown trout were carried above natural migration barriers into lakes they could not have colonised unaided, making the introduction deliberate rather than incidental
Wooden trap structures at Lake Tesse date from c. 5000 BCE, centuries before farming reached Scandinavia
The introduced populations are self-sustaining and still support fishing, so the modification has outlived every institution that made it

evidence.source: Mjærum, A. et al. (2026) Fish traps at Lake Tesse and Mesolithic translocation of brown trout in the southern Norwegian mountains, Antiquity
Radiocarbon dates on the wooden trap structures at Lake Tesse, placing use from c. 5000 BCE onward
Surveys of present-day brown trout (Salmo trutta) populations in upland lakes lying above waterfalls and rapids impassable to migrating fish

notes: Added August 2026. ethical_alignment is scored 0.65 rather than high, and that is deliberate: this is the earliest known deliberate species introduction, and species introduction is the mechanism behind a large share of modern ecological damage. The codex should not score a technology well merely because it is old and Indigenous. What earns the score it does get is that the intervention was legible, local, and has proved stable for seven millennia — which is more than can be said for most 19th-century acclimatisation programmes built on the same idea.
